final_task_tree.description: We're shipping a consumer mobile app that scans a user's face to verify identity at signup, and we charge a monthly subscription. Before launch I need to know, state by state, which biometric privacy laws apply to us, what notice and written consent we have to collect, how long we're allowed to retain the scan, whether there's a private right of action, and what the penalties are. Flag the states that are genuinely dangerous to launch in.

comments.body:
Starting on this. Scoping note before I break it down:

The 50-state framing is right for the *answer* but wrong for the *work*. Biometric-specific statutes with real teeth exist in a handful of states; the rest split into (a) comprehensive consumer privacy acts that treat biometrics as sensitive data requiring opt-in consent, and (b) states with no applicable regime beyond general UDAP/data-breach law. So I'm going to research in tiers rather than alphabetically, and the report will still give you a full 50-state disposition table.

Two things I'm flagging up front because they affect scope and I don't want to bury them:
1. Face scan *for identity verification* is a narrower use than face scan for identification/matching against a database, and several statutes turn on that distinction. I'll research it but the exact characterisation of your matching flow is an engineering question I'll leave you a subtask for.
2. The monthly subscription is a second, unrelated compliance surface (auto-renewal / negative option laws — CA ARL, FTC click-to-cancel). It's out of scope for a biometrics task but it's a genuine launch blocker, so I'll leave you a stub rather than silently dropping it.

Nothing I produce here is legal advice — this is a scoping document to make outside counsel cheaper and faster.

Done — report attached, tree built out. Here's where things stand.

**The headline**

Of 50 states: **1 can end the company** (Illinois), **3 more are seriously dangerous** (Texas, Washington, Colorado), **1 constrains product design** more than anyone else (Maryland), and the remaining 45 are documentation or nothing. Illinois is the outlier for exactly one reason — a private right of action with statutory damages, fee-shifting, and no need to prove harm. $1,000/user negligent, $5,000/user reckless. At 25,000 Illinois users a defective flow is $25M–$125M, and there's no partial exposure because one bad screen affects 100% of users.

**Four things I found that I think change how you'd approach this**

1. **Our exact product has already been sued twice.** Onfido settled ~$28.5M and Jumio ~$7M on selfie-IDV-at-signup. Two assumptions die there: "we only verify, we don't recognise" is not a defence, and the GLBA finance carve-out isn't available — Jumio tried it and lost at the pleading stage.

2. **On-device architecture is the highest-leverage move available.** G.T. v. Samsung and Zellmer v. Meta both support the position that you must actually possess the template to have "collected" it. If the match runs on-device and you store only a boolean, there's a strong argument BIPA never attaches. That's worth more than any consent screen, which is why I made it the first subtask and assigned it to you rather than guessing.

3. **Washington is the trap.** Everyone checks RCW 19.375, sees no private right of action, relaxes. Wrong statute twice: 19.375 probably doesn't even apply to us (its definition excludes photos *and data generated therefrom* — broader than BIPA's exclusion), while MHMDA *does* have a private right of action and no threshold. We're likely saved by its identity-theft/fraud exemption, but the burden is ours and the memo has to exist *before* a complaint arrives. Hence a dedicated subtask.

4. **Colorado has a scope trap.** HB 24-1130's biometric provisions apply with *no* consumer-count threshold, unlike the rest of the CPA. You're in scope at 100 users. Most summaries miss this.

**What I'd push back on, gently**

The brief asked for a state-by-state breakdown, and you've got one — but the 50-state framing slightly obscures the real shape. Most states are threshold-gated at 25k–100k users and don't apply at launch at all. The binding constraints on day one are only the no-threshold regimes: IL, TX (×2), NE, CO, WA. Build one flow to the Illinois standard, ship it everywhere, and you're covered as you scale without revisiting. I'd also **not geo-block Illinois** — it's leaky and the compliance work is cheap next to the exposure.

**11 subtasks waiting for you**, each self-contained. The two that gate everything: the **on-device decision** and the **counsel review of the Illinois notice text**. Items 3–6 (consent screen, consent logging, 30-day destruction, public policy page) are the minimum viable compliant launch and can run in parallel with counsel.

**One thing outside the brief I didn't drop:** the monthly subscription is a separate compliance surface (auto-renewal law — CA ARL, FTC click-to-cancel, state ARLs). I didn't research it since it's not biometrics, but it's a genuine launch blocker and it matters *here* because the subscription disclosure lives on the same signup screens you're about to rebuild. report.markdown:
# Biometric Privacy Compliance: 50-State Analysis
### Consumer mobile app — face scan for identity verification at signup

**Bottom line:** Of 50 states, **one** can end the company (Illinois), **three more** are seriously dangerous (Texas, Washington, Colorado), **one** constrains product design more than anyone else (Maryland), and the remaining 45 are documentation exercises or nothing at all. The total compliance work is roughly **two engineering weeks plus one legal review** — small relative to an exposure that runs into eight or nine figures if you skip it.

*Not legal advice. This is a scoping document to make outside counsel faster and cheaper, and it assumes templates reach our servers — the worse case.*

---

## 1. The decision that matters most: on-device vs server-side

Before anything else, resolve one engineering question, because it changes the entire risk profile.

Two 2024 decisions support the position that a company must **actually receive or possess** a biometric template to have "collected" it under BIPA:

- **G.T. v. Samsung** (N.D. Ill., July 2024) — BIPA claims dismissed; the court followed authority that a company must actually receive or access the data to "collect" it or be "in possession of" it. Directly aimed at companies whose software runs on the user's device.
- **Zellmer v. Meta** (9th Cir., June 17 2024) — summary judgment affirmed. Numeric "face signatures" from which no one can reconstruct facial features or identify anyone were held not to be biometric identifiers, and the plaintiff couldn't show the data was ever in Meta's possession.

**If the match happens on-device** and we store only a boolean `verified` plus a timestamp — no template, no embedding, no raw frames leaving the device — we have a strong, well-supported argument that BIPA §15 never attaches. That is worth more than any consent screen.

**If templates reach our servers,** we own the full burden and the full exposure. This is a defence, not immunity: it defeats liability, it doesn't prevent being named.

> Everything below assumes the server-side case. Resolve the architecture question first — an on-device answer materially shrinks the work.

---

## 2. Our exact product has already been sued — twice

This is not a hypothetical risk profile. Selfie-identity-verification-at-signup has produced two settlements on the precise theory that would be pled against us:

| Case | Settlement | Theory |
|---|---|---|
| **Sosa v. Onfido** (N.D. Ill., 20-cv-04247) | **~$28.5M** | Selfie IDV captured face geometry with no written notice of purpose or retention period and no written release. Survived motion to dismiss. |
| **Jumio** | **~$7M** | Materially the same informed-consent failure on selfie ID verification. |

Two conclusions follow, and both kill common assumptions:

1. **"We only verify identity, we don't do facial recognition" is not a defence.** BIPA covers a scan of face geometry regardless of whether you match against a database of strangers.
2. **The GLBA financial-institution exemption is not available to us.** Jumio raised it and lost at the pleading stage.

---

## 3. The four dangerous states

### 🔴 ILLINOIS — CRITICAL
**BIPA, 740 ILCS 14. No volume threshold — applies from user one.**

The only state where the downside is existential, for one reason: **a private right of action, with statutory damages, fee-shifting, and no requirement to prove actual harm** (*Rosenbach*). A bare procedural violation is actionable.

**What §15 requires, all before capture:**
- §15(b): inform in writing that biometric data is collected/stored; inform in writing of the **specific purpose and length of term**; obtain a **written release**
- §15(a): a **publicly available** written retention and destruction policy — destroy when purpose satisfied or within 3 years of last interaction, whichever is first
- §15(d): separate consent before disclosing to any third party

**Damages exposure** (post-SB 2979, one recovery per person per method):

| Illinois users | Negligent @ $1,000 | Reckless/intentional @ $5,000 |
|---|---|---|
| 5,000 | $5M | $25M |
| 25,000 | $25M | $125M |
| 100,000 | $100M | $500M |
| 500,000 | $500M | $2.5B |

Plus plaintiff attorneys' fees. Note there is no *partial* exposure — a defective consent flow is one systemic defect affecting 100% of enrolled users, and class certification is trivial because everyone saw the same screen.

**Two pieces of good news.** *Cothron v. White Castle* (2023) held a claim accrues on **every** scan, which was catastrophic; **SB 2979 (signed Aug 2 2024) legislatively overturned it** — repeat collection of the same identifier from the same person by the same method now yields a **single recovery**. Whether that applies retroactively is being fought over in the Seventh Circuit, but all of *our* conduct post-dates the amendment, so it's not our problem. SB 2979 also **expressly confirmed electronic signature satisfies "written release"** — defined as an electronic sound, symbol or process attached to or logically associated with a record and executed with intent to sign. No wet signature needed.

Also worth knowing: courts have held photographs are excluded from BIPA but a **face-geometry scan derived from a photograph is covered** (*Rivera v. Google*). A photo-based flow does not escape BIPA.

### 🟠 TEXAS — HIGH
**CUBI (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §503.001) + TDPSA + TRAIGA.**

Covers "record of hand or face geometry" — squarely us. No private right of action, but Texas is now **the most aggressive biometric enforcer in the country**: the AG extracted **$1.4 billion from Meta** over face tagging, and reads CUBI so that continued possession and use multiply violations, each carrying **up to $25,000**.

Texas also has the **tightest retention clock of any state**: destroy within a reasonable time after capture and **no later than one year after the purpose for collection expires**. For signup verification the purpose expires at verification, so this is a short fuse.

Texas reaches us three ways — CUBI, the **TDPSA (no volume threshold**, only an SBA small-business test), and **TRAIGA** (effective Jan 1 2026), which clarifies when someone is deemed to have consented to biometric capture and addresses biometric data used to train AI models.

### 🟠 WASHINGTON — HIGH, and the most commonly underestimated
Almost everyone checks **RCW 19.375**, sees no private right of action, and relaxes. That's the wrong statute twice over:

- **RCW 19.375 probably doesn't even apply to us.** Its definition of "biometric identifier" expressly excludes "a physical or digital photograph, video or audio recording **or data generated therefrom**." Broader than BIPA's exclusion — Washington excludes derived data, Illinois doesn't.
- **MHMDA (RCW 19.373) is the real risk.** It has a **private right of action** through the Consumer Protection Act with plaintiff-friendly presumptions, **no volume threshold**, and it lists biometric data as a category of consumer health status **with no use-based qualification** — so on a literal reading our scan is "consumer health data" despite having nothing to do with health. First class action filed **Feb 10 2025**.

**We are probably saved by an exemption.** MHMDA does not apply to information used to prevent, detect, protect against or respond to security incidents, **identity theft, fraud**, harassment, malicious or deceptive activity, or illegal activity. Signup identity verification sits squarely inside that limb.

Three conditions on relying on it: the **burden is on us** to demonstrate it applies; we must **document the reasoning contemporaneously**; and it is **use-scoped** — it evaporates the moment the same scan is used for model training, analytics or marketing.

### 🟠 COLORADO — HIGH on scope, not on penalty
**CPA as amended by HB 24-1130, in force July 1 2025.** No private right of action and ordinary AG penalties, so the damages tail is limited. It ranks high because of a **scope trap almost everyone misses**: the biometric provisions apply to **any** controller doing business in or targeting Colorado that processes biometric identifiers, **regardless of the CPA's usual 100,000-consumer threshold**. A pre-launch app with 100 users is fully in scope on day one. Consumer-facing collection also draws a heavier obligation set than employee collection.

Requires consent plus a written biometric policy (retention schedule, deletion guidelines, security-incident protocol, **annual review**, publicly available). Retention: destroy at the **earliest** of purpose satisfied / 24 months after last interaction / 45 days after an annual review finds it unnecessary.

### 🟡 MARYLAND — MEDIUM-HIGH (design constraint, not litigation risk)
**MODPA**, widely regarded as the strictest comprehensive act. No private right of action, so not dangerous in the litigation sense — but it constrains **product design** more than any other state:

- **Hard data minimisation** (§14-4607(B)): collection limited to what is reasonably necessary and proportionate to the **specific service the consumer requested**. Consent **cannot** widen this, unlike every other state where consent unlocks processing.
- **Outright ban on selling sensitive data, regardless of consent.** Strictest such rule in the country.
- Minors: flat ban on targeted advertising/sale for under-18s using a **"knew or should have known"** standard, not actual knowledge.

MODPA is the reason "store the template so we can reuse it later" is not available to us.

---

## 4. Why the other 45 states are manageable

**No state except Illinois and Washington gives consumers a private right of action reaching a consent failure.** California's is breach-only. Everywhere else it's an AG fine, typically capped at $7,500 per violation, often with a 30-day cure period that lets you fix a defect before penalty.

The ~20 comprehensive-privacy-act states all resolve to the **same requirement set**: opt-in consent for sensitive data (biometrics always qualify), a privacy notice, a DPIA, and data minimisation. An Illinois-grade flow satisfies every one of them automatically, because their consent standard is ordinary affirmative opt-in rather than a signed written release.

**Most are threshold-gated and won't apply at launch scale:**

| Threshold | States |
|---|---|
| **No threshold at all** | **Texas (TDPSA), Nebraska (NDPA)** — SBA small-business test only |
| 25,000–35,000 | Montana (25k), Maryland, New Hampshire, Delaware, Rhode Island (35k) |
| 50,000 | Minnesota |
| 100,000 | Virginia, Connecticut, Colorado (general CPA), Oregon, New Jersey, Indiana, Kentucky, Tennessee |
| $25M revenue or 100k | California, Utah |
| $1B+ revenue | Florida — effectively never applies to us |

So at launch the binding constraints are the **no-threshold regimes**: Illinois BIPA, Texas CUBI + TDPSA, Nebraska NDPA, Colorado's biometric amendment, and Washington MHMDA. Build to the strictest standard now and you never revisit it as you scale.

**25 states have no applicable biometric regime at all.** The only residual duty there: **don't lie.** If the privacy policy says scans are deleted in 30 days, failing to do so is an actionable deceptive practice under every one of those states' UDAP statutes.

**Also worth noting:**
- **Nevada SB 370** covers biometric data as consumer health data but — critically, unlike Washington — has **no private right of action**. AG-only, deceptive-trade-practice framing.
- **Arkansas APDPA** (from July 1 2026) treats "biometric data used for identification" as sensitive, at **$10,000 per violation** — higher than the tier norm. Don't file Arkansas under "nothing to do."
- **New York** has no comprehensive law; the NYC Biometric Identifier Ordinance targets "commercial establishments" and its private right of action attaches mainly to *selling* biometrics. Likely outside our scope as a pure app, but confirm if we ever have physical premises or kiosks.
- **Watch list:** South Carolina (biometric-only bill pending), Massachusetts and Michigan (BIPA-style bills with private rights of action repeatedly introduced). A Massachusetts BIPA clone with a PRA would materially change this analysis.

---

## 5. What to build — minimum viable compliant launch

One flow, built to the Illinois standard, shipped in all 50 states. **Do not geo-fence the consent flow** — geo-detection is unreliable (VPNs, travel, relocation, bad IP data), being wrong in Illinois costs $1,000–$5,000 per user, and showing the strict flow to a Wyoming user costs nothing.

| # | Requirement | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Pre-capture** notice + **separate, unchecked** e-signature consent, never bundled into ToS | BIPA §15(b) is a pre-collection duty; post-capture consent violates it even if the user agrees |
| **2** | Versioned, immutable consent log — notice text version, UTC timestamp, method, app version, capture timestamp strictly after consent | This is the evidence that wins or loses the case. Must survive account deletion; keep 5+ years |
| **3** | **Destroy template within 30 days**, ideally immediately on verification. Keep only the outcome | Satisfies TX (1 yr), CO (24 mo/45 day), IL (3 yr), MD (minimisation) with wide margin |
| **4** | **Public** biometric retention policy page — no login required | BIPA §15(a) + Colorado. Cheapest requirement here and the most commonly missed — the standard bolt-on claim against companies that built the consent screen but never published the policy |
| **5** | **No secondary use** — no training, analytics, personalisation, ads, or sale | Preserves the WA MHMDA exemption and MD's sale ban; TRAIGA addresses biometric training data |
| **6** | Vendor terms: our retention schedule, no-training, verifiable deletion, BIPA indemnity | Courts let BIPA claims proceed against vendors *and* customers — both are exposed, not one instead of the other |
| **7** | WA exemption memo + one DPIA | Memo must be contemporaneous; one DPIA covers ~10 states at once |

**Notice copy must say:** that a scan of **face geometry** is collected and stored (use the word — not "photo check"); the **specific purpose**, stated narrowly as identity verification at signup; the **specific length of term**; any third-party recipient by name; that it will be permanently destroyed.

**Critically — do not pad the purpose.** Adding "and to improve our services" or "for security generally" breaks the Washington MHMDA exemption and undermines Maryland minimisation. Narrow purpose language is a compliance asset.

**Destruction must actually reach everything:** primary storage, backups, caches, application logs, crash dumps, analytics pipelines, and the vendor's copy. An undeleted template in a backup is still possession.

---

## 6. Recommendation

**Launch in all 50 states — after items 1–4 above are built and counsel has reviewed the Illinois notice text.**

Geo-blocking Illinois is the worse option: it's leaky, it forfeits a top-five state economy, and the compliance work is cheap next to the exposure. The only scenario where geo-blocking Illinois makes sense is an immovable launch date with the consent flow unfinished.

**Sequence:**
1. Resolve the on-device architecture question — it may shrink everything else *(assigned)*
2. Build items 1–4 in parallel with the counsel review *(assigned)*
3. Counsel reviews Illinois notice + consent text and the e-signature implementation *(assigned)*
4. Fix vendor contract terms if a vendor is in the flow *(assigned)*
5. Decide 18+ only — cheapest way to remove an entire compliance surface, and your IDV flow can double as age assurance *(assigned)*

**One flag outside this brief:** the monthly subscription creates a **second, unrelated compliance surface** — automatic-renewal / negative-option law (California ARL, the FTC click-to-cancel rulemaking whose status has been litigated, plus a patchwork of state ARLs). ARL claims are an active plaintiff area and often plead alongside privacy claims. It matters here for a practical reason: **the subscription disclosure has to live on the same signup screens you're about to rebuild for biometric consent** — so design them together or you'll do the work twice. Raised as its own task rather than buried here.

subtasks.title: Tier 1: Research dedicated biometric privacy statutes (IL, TX, WA, CO, plus any new for 2025-26)
subtasks.description:
The states with standalone biometric statutes. FINDINGS (verified against statute text / AG guidance):

**ILLINOIS — BIPA, 740 ILCS 14 (2008). THE critical state.**
- Covers "scan of hand or face geometry" + derived "biometric information". Statute excludes photographs, BUT courts have held a face-geometry scan DERIVED from a photograph IS covered (Rivera v. Google, N.D. Ill. 2017, MTD denied). A photo-based face scan does NOT escape BIPA.
- §15(b): before collection must (1) inform in writing that biometric data is being collected/stored, (2) inform in writing of the SPECIFIC PURPOSE and LENGTH OF TERM, (3) obtain a written release. All three, before capture.
- §15(a): PUBLICLY AVAILABLE written retention/destruction policy. Destroy when purpose satisfied OR within 3 years of last interaction, whichever is FIRST.
- §15(d): no third-party disclosure without separate consent — relevant if using an IDV vendor.
- Private right of action: YES. This is the single fact that makes Illinois different from every other biometric statute.
- Exemptions: GLBA financial institutions; government contractors.

**TEXAS — CUBI, Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §503.001 (2009).**
- Covers "record of hand or face geometry" — squarely includes face scans.
- Notice + consent required before capturing for a commercial purpose.
- RETENTION (confirmed, TX AG): destroy within a reasonable time after capture, and NO LATER THAN ONE YEAR after the purpose for collection expires. For signup identity verification the purpose expires essentially at verification, so this is the tightest practical clock of any state — materially shorter than BIPA's 3 years.
- Civil penalty up to $25,000 PER VIOLATION. AG has EXCLUSIVE enforcement; no private right of action.
- AG reads it aggressively — collection AND continued possession/use can multiply violations. Meta settled with TX AG for $1.4 BILLION over face tagging. Texas is now the most active AG enforcer in this space.

**WASHINGTON — RCW 19.375 (HB 1493, 2017). Weaker than it looks.**
- CRITICAL: "biometric identifier" EXPRESSLY EXCLUDES "a physical or digital photograph, video or audio recording or data generated therefrom." Broader than BIPA's exclusion — WA excludes data *derived from* photos, Illinois does not. If our scan is photo/video-derived there is a strong argument RCW 19.375 does not apply at all.
- Trigger is "enroll ... in a database for a commercial purpose"; "enroll" = convert into a reference template. Notice + consent OR a mechanism to prevent subsequent commercial use.
- Enforcement: AG only via Consumer Protection Act, up to $7,500/violation. NO private right of action.
- Exemptions: GLBA, HIPAA, law enforcement.
- DO NOT stop at RCW 19.375 for Washington — the My Health My Data Act (RCW 19.373) is a separate overlay WITH a private right of action. Covered in the exemptions subtask.

**COLORADO — CPA Biometric Amendment, HB 24-1130, in force July 1 2025.**
- SCOPE TRAP (confirmed): the biometric provisions apply to ANY controller doing business in / targeting Colorado that processes biometric identifiers, REGARDLESS of the CPA's usual thresholds (100k consumers / 25k + sale). A small pre-launch app is in scope on day one. This is the most commonly missed point about the Colorado regime.
- Consent required before collection/use. Written biometric policy required: retention schedule, deletion guidelines, security-incident protocol, annual review, publicly available.
- RETENTION: destroy at the EARLIEST of (a) purpose satisfied, (b) 24 months after last interaction, (c) 45 days after an annual review determines the data is no longer necessary. Stricter than BIPA.
- Consumer biometrics carry a heavier burden than employee biometrics under this amendment — we are consumer-facing, so we get the heavier set.
- Enforcement: AG / district attorneys. NO private right of action.

Also biometric-specific but narrower: NYC Biometric Identifier Ordinance (commercial establishments; private right of action attaches to SALE/sharing of biometrics); Portland OR ban on face recognition in places of public accommodation.

NET: three states impose a hard consent+policy+retention regime on us (IL, TX, CO), one is probably inapplicable on the photograph exclusion (WA §19.375) but dangerous via a different statute (MHMDA).

subtasks.title: Tier 2: Research comprehensive state privacy acts that classify biometrics as sensitive data
subtasks.description:
Comprehensive state privacy acts treating biometrics as SENSITIVE DATA. FINDINGS:

**The universal pattern.** ~20 states have comprehensive consumer privacy acts in force as of 2026. Nearly all of them: (a) define "biometric data" as SENSITIVE data; (b) require OPT-IN CONSENT before processing sensitive data; (c) require a privacy notice disclosing sensitive-data categories and purposes; (d) require a data protection impact assessment / DPIA for sensitive-data processing; (e) require data minimisation; (f) give enforcement to the AG only — NO private right of action; (g) penalties typically up to $7,500 per violation; (h) many have a 30-day cure period.
Crucially, the consent standard is ordinary affirmative opt-in — NOT Illinois' signed "written release." So a well-built consent screen satisfies all of them at once. These states are a documentation problem, not an existential one.

**THE THRESHOLD INSIGHT — this reorders the whole risk picture.**
Most of these acts only bite above a volume threshold, so at launch scale most do NOT apply yet:
- 100,000 consumers: Virginia, Connecticut, Colorado (general CPA), Oregon, Minnesota, New Jersey, Indiana, Kentucky, Tennessee (+ revenue test), Utah (+$25M revenue)
- 50,000: Minnesota (per one source — verify), Montana originally 50k, NOW LOWERED TO 25,000
- 35,000: Maryland, New Hampshire, Delaware, Rhode Island (MD/DE/RI also have a 10,000 + 20%-of-revenue-from-sale alternative)
- California CCPA/CPRA: $25M revenue OR 100k consumers OR 50%+ revenue from selling data
- Florida Digital Bill of Rights: $1 BILLION+ global revenue — effectively never applies to us
- **NO THRESHOLD AT ALL: TEXAS (TDPSA) and NEBRASKA (NDPA).** Both apply to any entity doing business in / targeting the state that processes personal data and is NOT an SBA-defined "small business." These two are in scope from day one if we outgrow SBA small-business status. Texas therefore hits us twice — CUBI *and* TDPSA.

=> Practical sequencing: at launch, the binding constraints are the no-threshold regimes (IL BIPA, TX CUBI, TX TDPSA, NE NDPA, CO biometric amendment, WA MHMDA). The 35k/100k states become live as we scale, so build the consent flow to the strictest standard now and you never have to revisit it.

**MARYLAND — MODPA (Md. Com. Law §14-4601), the strictest comprehensive act. Needs its own attention.**
- Took effect Oct 1 2025; does NOT apply to processing activities before April 1 2026; discretionary cure period for violations on or before April 1 2027.
- §14-4607(B) HARD DATA MINIMISATION: collection limited to what is "reasonably necessary and proportionate" to provide the SPECIFIC service the consumer requested. This is a substantive cap that consent CANNOT widen — unlike other states where consent unlocks processing. For us: collecting a face scan to verify identity at signup is defensible as necessary to the requested service; retaining the template afterwards, or reusing it for anything else, is much harder to defend.
- OUTRIGHT BAN on the SALE of sensitive data, REGARDLESS OF CONSENT. Strictest sensitive-data rule in the country. Never sell or share-for-value the face data. Note "sale" is defined broadly in these acts and can capture some ad-tech disclosures.
- Minors: flat ban on targeted advertising / sale for under-18s, using a "knew or should have known" standard rather than actual knowledge — effectively pushes toward some age assurance.
- Threshold 35,000 MD consumers (or 10,000 + >20% revenue from sale).

**OTHER STATE-SPECIFIC NOTES**
- **Texas TRAIGA / HB 149** (AI governance act, effective Jan 1 2026): applies privacy requirements to data processed for AI systems, CLARIFIES WHEN A PERSON IS DEEMED TO HAVE CONSENTED TO BIOMETRIC CAPTURE, and creates limited exceptions for biometric data used to train AI models. Directly relevant if the face-matching model is ever trained or tuned on user scans — flag for counsel.
- **Connecticut**: adds neural data to sensitive data from July 1 2026; CTDPA amendments effective July 1 2026 broaden scope. Cure period sunsetting.
- **California**: CCPA/CPRA treats biometric information as sensitive personal information, giving a right to LIMIT use. California's private right of action is narrow — it exists only for DATA BREACHES of certain unencrypted personal information (which does include biometric data), not for consent failures. So California is a breach-liability state, not a consent-litigation state. CPPA is an active, well-resourced regulator with rulemaking authority, which no other state has.
- **Colorado**: general CPA thresholds are irrelevant to us because the HB 24-1130 biometric provisions apply with NO threshold. See Tier 1.
- **Oregon**: notable for requiring disclosure of SPECIFIC third parties data was shared with, on request — a transparency burden if we use an IDV vendor.
- **Nebraska NDPA**: no threshold, SBA small-business test, otherwise tracks the Texas model.
- Indiana, Kentucky, Rhode Island all took effect Jan 1 2026; all require opt-in consent for sensitive data incl. biometric; Kentucky AG exclusive enforcement, 30-day cure, up to $7,500/violation.

NET: no private right of action in ANY of these (except California's narrow breach-only claim), penalties are per-violation AG fines usually capped at $7,500, and cure periods often let you fix a defect before penalty. Compared to BIPA, this whole tier is manageable. Maryland's minimisation rule and Texas's double coverage are the two things to actually engineer around.

subtasks.title: Tier 3: Confirm the remaining states have no applicable biometric regime
subtasks.description:
Disposition of the remaining states. FINDINGS:

**Arkansas moved UP a tier during research — do not file it under "nothing to do."**
- Arkansas Personal Data Privacy Act (APDPA) takes effect JULY 1 2026. Sensitive data expressly includes "genetic or biometric data used for identification" — which is exactly our use. AG enforcement, civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation (higher than the $7,500 typical of this tier). No private right of action.
- Separately, Ark. Code Ann. §4-110-103(7) has included biometric data within "personal information" for BREACH purposes since Act 1030 of 2019. Enforced via the Arkansas Deceptive Trade Practices Act, up to $10,000/violation; willful violations are a Class A misdemeanor.
- Arkansas also has a teen privacy law (Act of 2025) effective July 1 2026 requiring consent for 13–16 year olds on sites/apps directed at teens, with biometric data inside its definition of personal information.
=> Treat Arkansas as a Tier 2 state from July 1 2026.

**Nevada — health-data statute, but benign for us.**
- Nevada SB 370 (consumer health data, effective Mar 31 2024) is modelled on Washington MHMDA and covers biometric data. BUT, critically, it has NO PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION — violations are deemed a deceptive trade practice enforceable only by the Nevada AG (injunctive relief, civil penalties, remediation). This is the single most important difference from Washington. Nevada is a notice-and-consent documentation exercise, not a litigation risk.
- Nevada has no comprehensive privacy act.

**New York — no comprehensive act, but three live edges.**
- No comprehensive state privacy law in force.
- NYC Biometric Identifier Ordinance (NYC Admin Code §22-1201 et seq.): applies to "commercial establishments" (retail/food/entertainment venues) and requires conspicuous notice; it carries a private right of action, but it is directed at SELLING/sharing biometric data. A mobile app is likely outside "commercial establishment," but confirm with counsel if we ever have physical premises or kiosks.
- NY SHIELD Act imposes reasonable-security obligations on private information of NY residents, and NY passed a consumer-health-data law in the MHMDA family. Worth a counsel check but not a launch blocker.

**The 25 states with NO applicable biometric regime.**
Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Kansas, Louisiana, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Mississippi, Missouri, New Mexico, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Vermont, West Virginia, Wisconsin, Wyoming.
For each of these the disposition is the same: no biometric-specific statute, no comprehensive consumer privacy act in force, biometrics appear (in some) only inside the data-breach notification statute. Residual obligations are (a) breach notification if the biometric data is exposed, and (b) the state UDAP/deceptive-practices statute, which means our public privacy representations must be accurate — if our privacy policy says we delete scans in 30 days, failing to do so is an actionable deceptive practice in all 25.

**Watch list / pending**
- South Carolina: a bill in the House with fairly broad protections but scoped ONLY to biometric information. If it passes, SC jumps straight into Tier 1 territory. Worth monitoring.
- Massachusetts and Michigan have repeatedly introduced BIPA-style bills with private rights of action. Massachusetts is the one to watch most closely — a BIPA clone with a PRA in MA would be a material change to this analysis.
- Vermont has a data-broker registration law; not applicable to us as a first-party collector.

METHOD NOTE: verified the arithmetic covers all 50 — 20 comprehensive-act states + Arkansas (from July 2026) + Illinois/Washington (biometric or health specific, not comprehensive) + Nevada + New York + 25 no-regime = 50.

subtasks.title: Research the identity-verification carve-outs and exemptions that could reduce exposure
subtasks.description:
Carve-outs, exemptions and architecture options that could reduce exposure. FINDINGS — this is the most useful subtask in the tree, read it first.

**1. THE DIRECTLY ON-POINT PRECEDENT — selfie IDV at signup has already been sued, twice**
- Sosa v. Onfido (N.D. Ill., 20-cv-04247): ~$28.5M settlement. Allegation was precisely our flow — Onfido's selfie identity verification captured facial geometry without written notice of purpose or retention period and without a written release. Survived motion to dismiss.
- Jumio: ~$7M settlement on materially the same theory (selfie ID verification, informed-consent failure).
- Jumio argued BIPA's FINANCIAL INSTITUTION exemption and LOST at the pleading stage.
=> Conclusion: "we only use it to verify identity, not to identify people" is NOT a defence to BIPA, and the GLBA exemption is not available to us. There is no version of this where the Illinois consent flow is optional. Treat these two settlements as the base case for what a defective flow costs.

**2. ARCHITECTURE: on-device-only processing is the one genuinely strong risk reduction**
- G.T. v. Samsung (N.D. Ill., July 2024): claims dismissed. Court followed the line of authority that a company must ACTUALLY RECEIVE OR ACCESS the data to "collect" it or be "in possession of" it under BIPA. Significant specifically for companies whose software runs on the user's device and never handles the biometric server-side.
- Zellmer v. Meta (9th Cir., June 17 2024): affirmed summary judgment for Meta. Two useful holdings — (a) "face signatures" that are merely abstract numeric representations, from which no one can reconstruct facial features or identify anyone, are not biometric identifiers/information; (b) plaintiff failed to show the data was ever in Meta's possession.
- PRACTICAL IMPLICATION: if the face match happens entirely on-device, the template is never transmitted to or stored by us, and we retain only a boolean "verified: true" plus perhaps a non-reversible hash, we have a real and well-supported argument that BIPA §15(b)/(a) are not triggered at all. That is worth far more than any consent screen.
- CAVEAT: this is a defence, not immunity. It defeats liability at summary judgment, it does not stop you being named. And it collapses the moment any template touches your servers or a vendor's.

**3. WASHINGTON: the fraud/identity-verification exemption in MHMDA — probably saves us**
- MHMDA (RCW 19.373) is the dangerous Washington statute, not RCW 19.375, because it has a PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION via the Consumer Protection Act, with plaintiff-friendly presumptions. First class action filed Feb 10 2025.
- Bad news: MHMDA lists biometric data as a category of "consumer health status" with NO qualification or use-based exclusion, so on a literal reading biometric collection in ANY context is "consumer health data" — including ours, which has nothing to do with health.
- GOOD NEWS: MHMDA contains a targeted exemption for information used to prevent, detect, protect against or respond to security incidents, IDENTITY THEFT, FRAUD, harassment, malicious or deceptive activity, or illegal activity. Signup identity verification sits squarely inside that exemption.
- CONDITIONS: the burden is on us to demonstrate the exemption applies, so we must document contemporaneously why and to what extent it applies. And it is USE-SCOPED — if the same scan is also used for model training, analytics, personalisation or marketing, the exemption does not cover that secondary use and MHMDA snaps back on with its private right of action.
- MHMDA also has no revenue/volume threshold for applicability (the 100k/25k figures are a compliance-deadline distinction for small businesses, not an exemption).
- Also note MHMDA carves out data within GLBA/HIPAA/FCRA/SSA Title XI/FERPA scope, but as DATA-level not ENTITY-level exemptions.

**4. Fraud-prevention exceptions in the comprehensive privacy acts — do NOT over-rely on these**
Most comprehensive state acts contain a provision saying their obligations don't restrict a controller's ability to prevent/detect/respond to fraud and security incidents. These are generally framed as permissions to PROCESS notwithstanding other duties — they do not reliably dissolve the separate, affirmative requirement to obtain opt-in consent before processing SENSITIVE data, which is where biometrics sit. Assume the sensitive-data consent obligation survives the fraud exception unless counsel advises otherwise for a specific state.

**5. Employee vs consumer scope**
Several of these regimes (MHMDA's "consumer" definition; Colorado's biometric amendment) treat employees differently. Irrelevant to us — we are purely consumer-facing, and consumer-facing is consistently the more heavily regulated side.

**6. Vendor structure shifts nothing onto the vendor**
Courts have largely allowed BIPA claims against third-party biometric vendors to proceed even with no direct user relationship — which means both you AND your IDV vendor are exposed, not one instead of the other. Additionally BIPA §15(d) requires SEPARATE consent to DISCLOSE biometrics to a third party, so routing the scan through a vendor creates an extra consent obligation rather than removing one. Contractual indemnity from the vendor is worth having but does not reduce statutory exposure.

**BOTTOM LINE**: two moves matter, in this order. (1) Keep the face template on-device and never receive it — this is the only thing that meaningfully removes BIPA exposure. (2) If templates must reach our servers, run the full Illinois-grade consent flow everywhere and never use the scan for any purpose other than verification, which also preserves the Washington MHMDA exemption.

subtasks.title: Research BIPA damages exposure and the class-action settlement record
subtasks.description:
BIPA damages exposure. FINDINGS:

**Statutory damages (740 ILCS 14/20)**
- $1,000 per violation for NEGLIGENT violation
- $5,000 per violation for INTENTIONAL or RECKLESS violation
- or actual damages if greater
- PLUS reasonable attorneys' fees and costs, and injunctive relief. Fee-shifting is why the plaintiffs' bar is so active here.
- No requirement to prove actual harm (Rosenbach) — a bare procedural violation is actionable. This is what makes BIPA a strict-liability-with-a-bounty statute.
- Statute of limitations: 5 years (Tims v. Black Horse Carriers, 2023).
- Note: at least one court (Rogers) held the liquidated damages award is DISCRETIONARY rather than automatic, and the jury determines the number of violations. Slight mitigation, not a defence.

**The accrual question — this is the big number-mover**
- Cothron v. White Castle (2023 IL 128004): a separate claim accrues with EVERY scan or transmission without prior informed consent. White Castle's own estimate of its exposure under this reading ran into the billions.
- SB 2979, signed Aug 2 2024, legislatively overturned Cothron: a private entity that more than once collects or discloses the SAME biometric identifier from the SAME person via the SAME method is entitled to only a SINGLE recovery. Per-scan stacking is gone for conduct going forward.
- OPEN LITIGATION RISK: whether SB 2979 applies retroactively to pre-amendment conduct is actively contested and has reached the Seventh Circuit. For a NEW app launching now this is not our problem — all our conduct post-dates the amendment. Good news for us specifically.

**Exposure model for us (post-SB 2979: one recovery per user)**
Face scan at signup is a single collection via a single method, so exposure scales with the number of Illinois users enrolled without compliant consent, not with the number of scans.

| Illinois users | Negligent @ $1k | Reckless/intentional @ $5k |
|---|---|---|
| 5,000 | $5,000,000 | $25,000,000 |
| 25,000 | $25,000,000 | $125,000,000 |
| 100,000 | $100,000,000 | $500,000,000 |
| 500,000 | $500,000,000 | $2,500,000,000 |

Add plaintiff attorneys' fees on top. Note that a defective consent flow is a single systemic defect affecting 100% of enrolled users — there is no partial exposure. Class certification is straightforward because the flow is identical for everyone.

**Settlement record (calibration)**
- Facebook / Tag Suggestions: $650M, ~1.6M Illinois class members, at least $345 per claimant. Court rejected an earlier $550M as inadequate.
- Google Photos: $100M, roughly $140 per valid claim.
- Clearview AI: settled via an equity-stake structure after conventional damages proved unpayable.
- Over 2,000 BIPA suits filed. This is a mature, well-organised plaintiffs' bar with template complaints.

**How they plead against consumer apps**
The standard theory is a §15(b) claim (no written release / no written notice of specific purpose and retention term before capture) bundled with a §15(a) claim (no publicly available retention schedule). §15(a) is the cheap add-on that catches companies who did the consent screen but never published the policy — do not skip the public policy page.

CONCLUSION: BIPA is the only regime where our downside is company-ending rather than a fine. The mitigation is cheap (a compliant consent screen + a published retention policy) and the failure mode is catastrophic, so this is the highest return-on-effort work in the whole launch.

subtasks.title: Draft the consent flow and notice requirements spec
subtasks.description:
Consent flow + notice requirements spec. Built to the STRICTEST standard (Illinois BIPA §15) so one flow satisfies all 50 states. Hand this to engineering and design as-is.

**DESIGN PRINCIPLE**: build one flow to the Illinois standard and ship it in every state. Do NOT geo-fence the consent flow by state — geo-detection is unreliable (VPNs, travel, relocation, wrong IP geolocation), and being wrong in Illinois costs $1,000–$5,000 per user. The incremental cost of showing the strict flow to a Wyoming user is zero.

---
**R1 — TIMING (hard requirement)**
The notice and the consent must both be complete BEFORE the camera activates and before any face data is captured, processed or transmitted. Not after capture, not during, not on the same screen as the capture preview. BIPA §15(b) is a pre-collection duty; a post-capture consent is a violation even if the user then agrees.

**R2 — NOTICE SCREEN CONTENT (all must appear in writing, on screen, before capture)**
Must state, in plain language:
1. That a biometric identifier — specifically a scan of face geometry — is being COLLECTED and STORED. Use the words "face geometry" and "biometric"; do not obscure it as "photo check" or "selfie."
2. The SPECIFIC PURPOSE: verifying your identity at account signup. Purpose must be stated narrowly. Do not add "and to improve our services" or "and for security purposes generally" — broad purpose language destroys the Washington MHMDA fraud exemption and undermines Maryland minimisation.
3. The LENGTH OF TERM for which it will be collected, stored and used — a specific duration, not "as long as necessary." See R5.
4. Whether it is disclosed to any third party, and WHO. Name the IDV vendor if one is used.
5. That the biometric will be permanently destroyed at the end of the stated term, and how.
6. A link to the public retention policy (R6) and to the privacy notice.

**R3 — CONSENT ARTIFACT (the "written release")**
- Must be a SEPARATE, STANDALONE affirmative action. Not bundled into acceptance of the general Terms of Service or privacy policy. A single "I agree to the Terms" checkbox does NOT constitute a BIPA written release.
- Must be unchecked/inactive by default. No pre-ticked boxes, no implied consent from continuing.
- Electronic signature is EXPRESSLY sufficient in Illinois post-SB 2979 (Aug 2 2024), which defines electronic signature as "an electronic sound, symbol, or process attached to or logically associated with a record and executed or adopted by a person with the intent to sign the record." A tap-to-sign or typed-name control satisfies this. This resolves the old ambiguity — you do NOT need a wet signature.
- Must be refusable. There must be a path to decline. If face verification is genuinely mandatory to use the product, the decline path must at minimum abandon signup cleanly rather than proceeding to capture.

**R4 — WHAT TO LOG AND RETAIN AS PROOF (this is what wins or loses the case)**
For every user, store an immutable, timestamped consent record containing:
- user ID; UTC timestamp of consent; the EXACT VERSION of the notice text displayed (store the full rendered text or a content hash plus a versioned copy of the text); the consent method (e.g. tap-to-sign); app version and platform; and the timestamp of first biometric capture — which must be strictly AFTER the consent timestamp.
- Version every change to the notice text and keep all historical versions indefinitely, even after users are deleted. In litigation the question is "what exactly did this user see on this date," and you must be able to answer it years later. Retain consent records for at least the 5-year Illinois limitations period plus a margin — note this is a separate retention clock from the biometric data itself, and it is legitimate to keep the consent record after destroying the template.
- Consent records should survive account deletion for the same reason.

**R5 — RETENTION AND DESTRUCTION (strictest-state composite)**
Binding constraints found:
- Texas CUBI: destroy within a reasonable time, no later than 1 YEAR after the purpose expires.
- Colorado HB 24-1130: earliest of purpose satisfied / 24 months after last interaction / 45 days after an annual review finds it unnecessary.
- Illinois BIPA: purpose satisfied OR 3 years after last interaction, whichever is FIRST.
- Maryland MODPA: only what is reasonably necessary and proportionate to the requested service — consent cannot widen this.
=> RECOMMENDED POLICY: **destroy the face template immediately upon completion of the verification, and in no case later than 30 days after capture.** For signup identity verification the purpose is satisfied the moment verification succeeds or fails, so every one of the statutes above is satisfied with a wide margin, and there is nothing left to leak or to litigate over. Retain only the verification OUTCOME (boolean + timestamp + method), not the biometric.
- If the product later needs re-verification, re-capture rather than storing a template for reuse. Storing a template "in case we need it again" converts a 30-day exposure into a multi-year one and is the single most expensive design decision available.
- Implement destruction as an automated, logged, verifiable job. Log the destruction event per record. Include backups, caches, logs, crash dumps, analytics pipelines and the vendor's copy — an undeleted template in a backup is still possession.

**R6 — PUBLIC WRITTEN POLICY (BIPA §15(a) + Colorado)**
Publish a PUBLICLY ACCESSIBLE written biometric retention policy — reachable without logging in, no account required. Must contain the retention schedule and the guidelines for permanent destruction. Colorado additionally requires a security-incident response protocol and an annual review; include both. This is the cheapest requirement in the whole task and it is the most commonly missed — it is the standard bolt-on claim in BIPA complaints against companies that did build a consent screen.

**R7 — NO SECONDARY USE (protects two separate exemptions)**
Never use the face scan or template for: model training or tuning, analytics, personalisation, advertising, age estimation, demographic inference, or any purpose beyond the specific verification. Never SELL or share-for-value biometric data — Maryland MODPA bans sale of sensitive data OUTRIGHT regardless of consent. Secondary use also breaks the Washington MHMDA fraud/identity-theft exemption we are relying on, and Texas TRAIGA (effective Jan 1 2026) specifically addresses biometric data used to train AI models. Enforce this as an engineering control and a written internal policy, not just an intention.

**R8 — VENDOR TERMS (if using a third-party IDV provider)**
- BIPA §15(d) requires SEPARATE consent to DISCLOSE biometrics to a third party. Either name the vendor in the R2 notice and cover disclosure in the R3 consent, or add a second consent for disclosure.
- Contract must: bind the vendor to our retention schedule; prohibit vendor use for its own model training (a common default in IDV vendor terms — check this specifically); require verifiable deletion with evidence; include BIPA-specific indemnity.
- Do not assume the vendor absorbs the risk. Courts have let BIPA claims proceed against both the customer-facing company and the vendor, and Onfido (~$28.5M) and Jumio (~$7M) both settled claims on this exact product pattern.

**R9 — DOCUMENT THE WASHINGTON EXEMPTION**
Write and retain a short contemporaneous memo recording why the face scan qualifies for MHMDA's identity-theft/fraud-prevention exemption and confirming the use is limited to that purpose. The burden of demonstrating the exemption is on us, so the memo must exist BEFORE launch, not be reconstructed after a complaint.

**R10 — DPIA / assessments**
Most comprehensive acts require a data protection impact assessment for sensitive-data processing. Write one DPIA covering the face-scan flow; it satisfies Virginia, Connecticut, Colorado, Oregon, Minnesota, New Jersey, Maryland, Texas and others simultaneously. Colorado requires annual review of the biometric retention schedule — calendar it.

**R11 — MINORS**
If under-18s can sign up, Maryland applies a "knew or should have known" standard (not actual knowledge) and flatly bans targeted advertising / sale of their data; Arkansas's teen law (from July 1 2026) requires consent for 13–16 year olds. Either block under-18 signup outright or get counsel input on age assurance. Simplest safe answer at launch: 18+ only, enforced at signup.

---
**MINIMUM VIABLE COMPLIANT LAUNCH — the short list**
1. Standalone pre-capture notice + separate unchecked e-signature consent (R1–R3)
2. Versioned immutable consent logging (R4)
3. Destroy template within 30 days, keep only the outcome (R5)
4. Public biometric retention policy page (R6)
5. No secondary use, contractually and technically enforced (R7)
6. Vendor terms fixed if a vendor is used (R8)
7. Washington exemption memo + one DPIA (R9, R10)

subtasks.title: Produce the 50-state disposition table and danger ranking
subtasks.description:
The 50-state disposition table and danger ranking. DONE — full alphabetical table is in the report attached to the parent task. Danger ranking and reasoning below.

**THE FOUR STATES THAT ARE GENUINELY DANGEROUS**

1. **ILLINOIS — CRITICAL. The only state where the downside is company-ending.**
Sole reason: a private right of action with statutory damages and fee-shifting, and no need to prove actual harm. $1,000/user negligent, $5,000/user reckless. At 25,000 Illinois users a defective flow is $25M–$125M. Our exact product pattern has already produced settlements (Onfido ~$28.5M, Jumio ~$7M). Requires a signed/e-signed written release, which no other state does. Do not launch in Illinois without the full flow built and counsel sign-off on the notice text.

2. **TEXAS — HIGH. Highest per-violation ceiling and the most aggressive regulator.**
$25,000 per violation under CUBI; the AG reads violations to multiply across continued possession; the AG extracted $1.4 BILLION from Meta over face tagging. No private right of action, but Texas is the most active biometric enforcer in the country right now. Texas also reaches us through TDPSA (no volume threshold) and TRAIGA. Tightest retention clock of any state — destroy no later than 1 year after the purpose expires.

3. **WASHINGTON — HIGH, and the most commonly underestimated.**
Everyone checks RCW 19.375, sees no private right of action, and relaxes — and in fact 19.375 may not even apply to us because its definition excludes photographs "and data generated therefrom." The real risk is MHMDA (RCW 19.373): private right of action via the Consumer Protection Act with plaintiff-friendly presumptions, no volume threshold, and biometric data listed as consumer health data with no use-based qualification. First class action filed Feb 2025. We are probably saved by MHMDA's identity-theft/fraud-prevention exemption — but the burden of proving it is ours, it must be documented in advance, and it evaporates on any secondary use.

4. **COLORADO — HIGH on scope, not on penalty.**
No private right of action and ordinary AG penalties, so the damages tail is limited. It ranks high because of the scope trap: HB 24-1130's biometric provisions apply with NO consumer-count threshold, unlike the rest of the CPA. A pre-launch app with 100 users is fully in scope on day one, and consumer-facing collection draws the heavier obligation set. Also imposes a full written-policy regime with annual review.

**SECOND TIER — MEDIUM-HIGH**
**Maryland (MODPA)** — strictest comprehensive act. Hard data minimisation that consent CANNOT override, plus an outright ban on selling sensitive data regardless of consent. No private right of action, so not dangerous in the litigation sense, but it constrains PRODUCT DESIGN more than any other state — it is the reason "store the template for later reuse" is not available to us.

**WHY EVERYTHING ELSE IS MANAGEABLE**
- No state other than Illinois and Washington gives consumers a private right of action that reaches a consent failure. California's is breach-only.
- The other ~20 comprehensive-act states all resolve to the same requirement set — opt-in consent for sensitive data, privacy notice, DPIA, minimisation — satisfied automatically by an Illinois-grade flow.
- Most are threshold-gated (25k–100k consumers) and do not apply at launch scale at all.
- 25 states have no applicable biometric regime whatsoever. The only residual duty there is not lying: published privacy claims must be true or the state UDAP statute is engaged.

**RISK DISTRIBUTION ACROSS THE 50**
CRITICAL 1 (IL) · HIGH 3 (TX, WA, CO) · MEDIUM-HIGH 1 (MD) · MEDIUM 7 · LOW-MEDIUM 10 · LOW 28 (incl. 3 on the watch list and FL out of scope)

**LAUNCH RECOMMENDATION**
Launch in all 50 states, but only after the R1–R6 minimum flow in the consent spec is built and counsel has reviewed the Illinois notice text. Geo-blocking Illinois is a worse option than complying — it is leaky (VPNs, travel, relocation), it forfeits a top-five state economy, and the compliance work is cheap relative to the exposure. The only scenario where geo-blocking Illinois makes sense is an immovable launch date with the consent flow not ready.

**WATCH LIST**: South Carolina (biometric-only bill pending), Massachusetts and Michigan (BIPA-style bills with private rights of action repeatedly introduced). A Massachusetts BIPA clone with a PRA would materially change this analysis.

subtasks.title: DECIDE: can the face match run entirely on-device, so no template ever reaches our servers?
subtasks.description:
This is the highest-leverage decision in the whole launch and it gates most of the work below. If the match happens on-device and we only ever store a boolean 'verified' + timestamp (no template, no raw image, no embedding), then per G.T. v. Samsung (N.D. Ill. 2024) and Zellmer v. Meta (9th Cir. 2024) we have a strong argument we never 'collected' or 'possessed' a biometric identifier and BIPA §15 is not triggered at all. That converts our single company-ending risk into a manageable one.

If templates DO reach our servers (or a vendor's), we own the full compliance burden and the full exposure: Onfido settled ~$28.5M and Jumio ~$7M on exactly this product pattern.

What you need to establish with engineering:
- Does the chosen SDK/vendor do matching locally or server-side?
- Does any raw image, frame, embedding or template leave the device, even transiently, even in logs/crash dumps/analytics?
- Can we architect to send only a pass/fail result?
- If a vendor is involved, does their pipeline require server-side processing by design?

Record the answer here, then tell me and I can re-scope the remaining compliance work — an on-device answer materially shrinks it.

NOTE: this is a defence, not immunity. It defeats liability, it does not prevent being named as a defendant.

subtasks.title: Get outside privacy counsel to review the Illinois BIPA notice + consent text before launch
subtasks.description:
The one piece of this that genuinely needs a lawyer, because Illinois is the only state where getting it wrong is company-ending ($1,000/user negligent, $5,000/user reckless, plus plaintiff attorneys' fees, no actual harm required).

What to send counsel:
- The consent flow spec (subtask 'Draft the consent flow and notice requirements spec' in this tree) — requirements R1 through R11
- The actual draft notice screen copy and the consent control design
- The proposed 30-day retention policy and the public policy page draft
- Confirmation of whether the architecture is on-device or server-side (see the decision subtask above)

Specific questions worth paying for:
1. Does our notice satisfy BIPA §15(b)'s 'specific purpose and length of term' in writing?
2. Is our e-signature implementation a valid 'written release' post-SB 2979 (which defines electronic signature as an electronic sound, symbol or process attached to or logically associated with a record and executed with intent to sign)?
3. If we use an IDV vendor, do we need a separate §15(d) consent to disclose, or does naming the vendor in the main notice suffice?
4. Does the on-device architecture (if adopted) take us outside §15(b) entirely, per the G.T. v. Samsung line of authority?
5. Any Illinois-specific exposure from the subscription/auto-renewal side interacting with the biometric consent.

Ask for a written opinion, not a call — you want something to point at later. Look for a firm with actual BIPA defence experience; this is a specialised bar.

subtasks.title: Build the pre-capture notice screen and standalone consent control
subtasks.description:
Implements requirements R1, R2 and R3 from the consent flow spec in this tree. Read that subtask's description for the full detail — summary here.

- Notice and consent must BOTH complete BEFORE the camera activates. BIPA §15(b) is a pre-collection duty; post-capture consent is a violation even if the user agrees.
- Notice must state in writing: that a scan of FACE GEOMETRY (use that word) is being collected and stored; the specific purpose (identity verification at signup, stated narrowly — do NOT add 'and to improve our services', that breaks the Washington MHMDA exemption and Maryland minimisation); the specific length of term; any third-party disclosure and who; that it will be permanently destroyed; links to the public retention policy and privacy notice.
- Consent must be a SEPARATE standalone affirmative action, NOT bundled into Terms of Service acceptance. Unchecked by default. No pre-ticked boxes, no implied consent from continuing.
- Must be refusable with a clean abandon path.
- Ship this flow in ALL 50 states. Do not geo-fence it by state — geo-detection is unreliable and being wrong in Illinois costs $1k-$5k per user, while showing the strict flow to a Wyoming user costs nothing.

subtasks.title: Build versioned immutable consent logging
subtasks.description:
Implements requirement R4 of the consent spec. This is the evidence that wins or loses a BIPA case — without it you cannot prove consent and are effectively strictly liable.

Per user, store immutably: user ID; UTC consent timestamp; the EXACT VERSION of notice text displayed (full rendered text or content hash + versioned copy of that text); consent method; app version and platform; and the timestamp of first biometric capture, which must be strictly AFTER the consent timestamp.

Critical details people get wrong:
- Version every change to the notice text and keep ALL historical versions indefinitely. In litigation the question is 'what exactly did this user see on this date' and you must answer it years later.
- Consent records must SURVIVE account deletion and survive destruction of the biometric template. This is a separate retention clock from the biometric data — retain at least 5 years (the Illinois limitations period) plus margin.
- Make the log append-only / tamper-evident.

subtasks.title: Implement automated 30-day template destruction with logged proof
subtasks.description:
Implements requirement R5 of the consent spec.

RECOMMENDED POLICY: destroy the face template immediately on completion of verification, and in no case later than 30 days after capture. Retain only the verification OUTCOME (boolean + timestamp + method), never the biometric.

This single policy satisfies every state's retention rule with a wide margin: Texas CUBI (≤1 year after purpose expires — the tightest), Colorado HB 24-1130 (earliest of purpose satisfied / 24 months after last interaction / 45 days post-annual-review), Illinois BIPA (purpose satisfied or 3 years, whichever first), Maryland MODPA (reasonably necessary and proportionate only).

Implementation requirements:
- Automated job, not a manual process
- Log each destruction event per record so you can prove it happened
- Destruction must reach: primary storage, backups, caches, application logs, crash dumps, analytics pipelines, and any vendor-side copy. An undeleted template in a backup is still possession.
- If re-verification is needed later, RE-CAPTURE. Do not store a template for reuse — that converts a 30-day exposure into a multi-year one and is the most expensive design decision available to us.

subtasks.title: Publish the public biometric retention policy page
subtasks.description:
Implements requirement R6. Cheapest requirement in the entire task and the single most commonly missed — it is the standard bolt-on claim in BIPA complaints against companies that DID build a consent screen but never published the policy.

Requirements:
- Publicly accessible with NO login and NO account required
- Must contain the retention schedule and the guidelines for permanent destruction (BIPA §15(a))
- Colorado HB 24-1130 additionally requires a security-incident response protocol and an annual review commitment — include both so one page covers both states
- Calendar the Colorado annual review of the retention schedule as a recurring task

This is a short page. It should take under an hour once the retention policy is settled.

subtasks.title: Write the Washington MHMDA exemption memo before launch
subtasks.description:
Implements requirement R9. Must exist BEFORE launch — the burden of demonstrating the exemption is on us, and a memo reconstructed after a complaint arrives is worth much less than a contemporaneous one.

Washington MHMDA (RCW 19.373) has a private right of action via the Consumer Protection Act with plaintiff-friendly presumptions, no volume threshold, and it lists biometric data as consumer health data with no use-based qualification — so on a literal reading our face scan is 'consumer health data' despite having nothing to do with health.

Our defence is MHMDA's exemption for information used to prevent, detect, protect against or respond to security incidents, IDENTITY THEFT, FRAUD, harassment, malicious or deceptive activity, or illegal activity. Signup identity verification sits squarely inside it.

The memo should record: (1) the precise purpose of the scan; (2) why that purpose falls within the identity-theft/fraud limb of the exemption; (3) an affirmative statement that the data is NOT used for any other purpose; (4) the technical controls enforcing that limitation; (5) date and author.

The exemption is USE-SCOPED — it dies the moment the scan is also used for model training, analytics, personalisation or marketing. Keep the memo accurate as the product evolves.

subtasks.title: Write one DPIA covering the face-scan flow
subtasks.description:
Implements requirement R10. Most comprehensive state privacy acts require a data protection impact assessment for sensitive-data processing. ONE well-written DPIA satisfies Virginia, Connecticut, Colorado, Oregon, Minnesota, New Jersey, Maryland, Texas, Indiana, Kentucky, Rhode Island and others simultaneously — this is a single document, not fifty.

Should cover: the categories of data processed (face geometry template, raw capture frames); purpose (identity verification at signup); necessity and proportionality assessment (important for Maryland MODPA's hard minimisation rule); retention and destruction; recipients including any vendor; security safeguards; risks to consumers and mitigations; and the balancing conclusion.

Most state templates are similar enough that a single document written to the Colorado/Maryland standard covers the field. Reuse the content from the exemption memo and retention policy rather than starting fresh.

subtasks.title: Fix IDV vendor contract terms — retention, no-training, deletion proof, BIPA indemnity
subtasks.description:
Implements requirement R8. Only needed if a third-party identity verification vendor (Persona, Onfido, Jumio, Veriff, Socure etc.) is in the flow. Skip if verification is fully first-party and on-device.

Why this matters: courts have allowed BIPA claims to proceed against third-party biometric vendors even with no direct user relationship, which means BOTH we and the vendor are exposed, not one instead of the other. Onfido settled ~$28.5M and Jumio ~$7M on this exact product pattern. Contractual indemnity is worth having but does NOT reduce statutory exposure.

Contract must:
- Bind the vendor to OUR retention schedule (30 days) and require verifiable deletion WITH EVIDENCE
- PROHIBIT vendor use of our users' biometric data for the vendor's own model training or product improvement. Check this specifically — permissive training rights are a common default in IDV vendor terms and directly conflict with our no-secondary-use position and with Texas TRAIGA.
- Include BIPA-specific indemnity and a defence obligation
- Confirm whether the vendor's pipeline requires server-side processing by design (feeds into the on-device decision subtask)

Separately: BIPA §15(d) requires SEPARATE consent to DISCLOSE biometrics to a third party. Either name the vendor in the main notice and cover disclosure in the consent, or add a second consent — confirm which with counsel.

subtasks.title: Decide whether under-18 signup is permitted, and block it if not
subtasks.description:
Implements requirement R11. Needs a product decision from you.

If minors can sign up, extra obligations attach:
- Maryland MODPA uses a 'knew or should have known' standard rather than actual knowledge, and flatly BANS targeted advertising and sale of under-18 data regardless of consent. The 'should have known' standard means you cannot simply avoid asking — contextual signals count, which effectively pushes toward some form of age assurance.
- Arkansas's teen privacy law (effective July 1 2026) requires consent from the teen or a parent for 13-16 year olds on services directed at teens, and includes biometric data in its definition of personal information.
- Several other states have youth-specific 2026 obligations (Virginia daily limits, Texas age verification, Arkansas and Oregon restrictions).

SIMPLEST SAFE ANSWER AT LAUNCH: restrict to 18+, enforced at signup, and state it in the terms. This removes a whole compliance surface for near-zero product cost, and there is a neat synergy — you are already running identity verification, which can double as age assurance.

If under-18 signup is commercially necessary, this needs its own counsel conversation and should be added to the counsel review subtask.

subtasks.title: Separately scope subscription auto-renewal compliance (out of scope here, but a real launch blocker)
subtasks.description:
FLAGGING, NOT RESEARCHING — this is outside the biometric brief but it is a genuine launch blocker for a monthly-subscription consumer app, and I did not want to silently drop it.

The monthly subscription creates a second, unrelated compliance surface: negative-option / automatic-renewal law. Known pressure points:
- California Automatic Renewal Law (recently strengthened) — clear and conspicuous pre-purchase disclosure, affirmative consent to the recurring charge, easy online cancellation in the same medium as signup, renewal reminders for longer terms
- FTC negative-option / 'click-to-cancel' rulemaking at federal level — note the rule's status has been litigated, so confirm where it currently stands before relying on it either way
- A patchwork of other state ARL statutes (NY, OR, CO, and others) with their own disclosure and cancellation-path rules
- App-store billing rules interact with all of this and may satisfy some requirements automatically if you bill through Apple/Google rather than direct

Why it matters here: ARL claims are a very active plaintiff area and often plead alongside privacy claims, so the same complaint can carry both. Also, the signup flow you are about to build for biometric consent is the SAME screen real estate where the subscription disclosure has to live — build them together rather than retrofitting, or you will do the flow twice.

Suggest raising this as its own top-level task so it gets proper research rather than living as a footnote under a biometrics task. Happy to take it if you assign it.
